paras: The attempted lynching of John Clements took place at West Point, King William County, Virginia, on the night of December 12, 1903, when white residents seized Clements, a Black man accused of shooting the white dairyman George Hobough, and, by one account, put a rope around his neck. He was handed to officers, and Hobough died in a Richmond hospital on December 23. Convicted of first-degree murder, Clements was legally hanged on March 11, 1904, an execution wire reports noted mainly for his baptism in the box that carried his body to a medical college.

The Richmond Times-Dispatch described Clements as a "Baltimore negro" employed in West Point as an oyster shucker. According to the white papers, Clements insulted Hobough on the street that evening and Hobough knocked him down. The Times-Dispatch added that Black onlookers were about to come to Clements's aid until a butcher named Pilcher held them off with a cleaver.

After dark, Clements was said to have met Hobough with a revolver that misfired several times as the unarmed man retreated. Two shots struck Hobough, in the back and the hip, the second reportedly fired after he fell inside a doorway, and Clements fled.

A posse of citizens armed with shotguns set out in every direction from town. In the Times-Dispatch version, two of the men met Clements on the railway toward Richmond, recognized his voice and arrested him at gunpoint. The Alexandria Gazette, headlining "TRIED TO LYNCH HIM," said instead that the "white population" caught him out of town and "had a rope around his neck" until "a few steady heads" prevailed. The Fredericksburg Free Lance reported that the people were restrained from lynching him only "with difficulty."

Asked for a plea before a magistrate, Clements answered, "That is for the court to decide." A strong posse took him to the jail at King William Courthouse, from which, the Gazette said, high feeling led to his removal to Hanover County.

Hobough was reported on December 22 to be doing nicely at the Virginia Hospital but died there the next morning. In an ante-mortem statement to Detective Captain Tomlinson he repeated that he had knocked Clements down for an insult and that Clements returned with a pistol. Coroner Taylor's inquest on December 24 found that Hobough died of bullet wounds made by Clements.

At the King William circuit court a jury deliberated about twenty minutes before finding Clements guilty of first-degree murder, and on February 6, 1904, he was sentenced to hang. The Times-Dispatch first said he had no counsel, but a letter from B. C. Garrett stated that the court had appointed A. Julian Bagby of West Point to defend him after two continuances. Clements was hanged at King William Court House on March 11, 1904, after being baptized by immersion in the box in which his body was then shipped to a Richmond medical college.

The Times-Dispatch gave the fullest December account under the headlines "SHOT DOWN BY A NEGRO" and "WAS DANGER OF LYNCHING." It called the shooting a "murderous assault" and credited "the cool judgment of influential citizens" with preventing "summary justice," while predicting that Clements faced "a fate almost as certain" if Hobough died. The Free Lance headlined "NEGRO ESCAPES LYNCHING" with "West Point People Wanted Revenge," though it alone qualified the attack with "it is charged." None of the December reports criticized the pursuers; each presented the averted lynching as the work of restraining citizens.

The hanging reached a wider audience through a Richmond wire printed in Birmingham, Savannah and Perth Amboy, New Jersey, which dwelt on the coffin baptism and omitted the lynching attempt. The only Black-press item, in the Savannah Tribune of March 19, 1904, copied that dispatch as "BAPTIZED IN HIS GOFFIN," subtitled "Murderer Goes Through Unique Ceremonial," without comment. No Black-press report of the December shooting or the lynching attempt appears in the coverage.

The rope appears only in the Gazette, while the Times-Dispatch, the Free Lance and Hobough's statement speak of a lynching threatened or narrowly restrained. Reports also differ on whether Clements was held at Hanover or in the King William jail, and on whether the back wound struck the liver or a lung.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of John Clements
bases: Pursuers seized John Clements after the shooting and, per the Gazette, put a rope around his neck before he was handed to officers; other papers say a lynching was threatened and narrowly prevented (A1, A2, A3, A6).

A crowd of white citizens tried or threatened to lynch Clements for the shooting but was stopped, and he was later tried and legally hanged (A1, A2, A8, A11); no one was killed by a mob, so this was an attempted lynching, not a lynching.

The Alexandria Gazette, the Richmond Times-Dispatch, the Fredericksburg Free Lance and Hobough's reported ante-mortem statement all describe a threatened lynching averted after the shooting (A1, A2, A3, A6); only the Gazette reports the rope (A1).

accounts.gist: Two posse members met Clements on the railway in the dark and arrested him at gunpoint; influential citizens prevented summary justice and a strong posse took him to the county jail.

accounts.label: Alexandria Gazette report
accounts.gist: The white population caught Clements out of town and had a rope around his neck before a few steady heads prevailed; he was later moved to Hanover for safety.

accounts.label: Hobough's ante-mortem statement
accounts.gist: Hobough said Clements insulted him, he knocked Clements down, and Clements returned with a pistol and shot him twice; threats of lynching followed.

accounts.label: Richmond wire on the hanging
accounts.gist: Clements was hanged at King William Court House after being baptized by immersion in the box in which his body was shipped to a medical college.

framing.detail: The Times-Dispatch headlined 'SHOT DOWN BY A NEGRO' and 'WAS DANGER OF LYNCHING', called the shooting a 'murderous assault' and praised the 'cool judgment of influential citizens' for preventing 'summary justice'.
The Free Lance headlined 'NEGRO ESCAPES LYNCHING' with 'West Point People Wanted Revenge', while qualifying the attack with 'it is charged'.
The Gazette's 'TRIED TO LYNCH HIM' blamed Clements for arousing citizens 'to a state of frenzy' and credited 'a few steady heads'.
In March the Richmond wire on the hanging ran under headlines about the coffin baptism, with no mention of the lynching attempt.
The Savannah Tribune copied the wire as 'BAPTIZED IN HIS GOFFIN' with the subhead 'Murderer Goes Through Unique Ceremonial', without comment.
